[Textbook misprint: the printed page labels the four options \((A)\ 25\ \text{W}\), \((C)\ 40\ \text{W}\), \((C)\ 60\ \text{W}\), \((D)\ 100\ \text{W}\) — label \((C)\) appears twice and \((B)\) is absent. The four option TEXTS and their printed order are preserved exactly; only the second label has been corrected to \((B)\), following the across-then-down layout the book itself uses in Q.1 (iv). The relabelling cannot move the answer, which is the 100 W option either way.]

At a fixed \(V = 230\) V the resistance is \(R = V^2/P\), so it falls as the power rises: \(2116\), \(1322.5\), \(881.7\) and \(529\ \Omega\) for the 25, 40, 60 and 100 W lamps, the smallest being that of the 100 W lamp.

Section 11.6 names liquid electrolytes, vacuum tubes and junction devices as non-ohmic, their \(I\)-\(V\) curve not being a straight line, whereas the metallic nichrome wire has a constant resistance and follows the linear characteristic of section 11.5.

Section 11.8.1 defines a rheostat as an adjustable resistor whose sliding contact varies the resistance continuously and by an uncalibrated amount, whereas a plug-type resistance box is what supplies a known change and a key is what makes and breaks the circuit.

Stretching conserves the volume, so halving the radius quarters the area and quadruples the length, giving \(R' = \rho(4L)/(A/4) = 16R\); the \(4R\) alternative would require the length to stay at \(L\), which stretching forbids.

For one metal \(m \propto Al\), so \(A \propto m/l\) and \(R = \rho l/A \propto l^2/m\), giving \(25 : 3 : 1/5\), that is \(125 : 15 : 1\); interchanging \(l\) and \(m\) is what produces the reversed \(1 : 15 : 125\).

Eq. 11.42 gives \(I = \varepsilon/(R + r) = 2/1.0 = 2\) A, so the terminal p.d. is \(V = \varepsilon - Ir = 2 - 0.2 = 1.8\) V; \(1.95\) V would require \(I = 0.5\) A and \(3\) V exceeds the emf, which no cell can do while driving a current.

With \(m\) rows of \(n = 100/m\) cells, \(I = n\varepsilon/(R + nr/m)\) is largest when \(nr/m = R\), i.e. \(n/m = 25\), which with \(mn = 100\) gives \(m = 2\); evaluating each printed alternative yields \(5\) A for two rows against \(4\), \(3.45\) and \(0.20\) A for four, five and one hundred rows.

The diagram shows five cells in one series line with the THIRD one reversed (its short negative plate and minus label face left while the other four face right), so the net emf is \(1.5(4 - 1) = 4.5\) V; five equal cells in series can only yield \(\pm 7.5\), \(\pm 4.5\) or \(\pm 1.5\) V, so neither \(0\) V nor \(6.0\) V is reachable by any arrangement at all.
